title: Why we chant
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart takes up the question of why Red Cedar Zen Community chants, opening with a Mary Oliver poem and the memory of Kanho's first visit, when the Heart Sutra and the Enmei Jukku Kannon Gyo arrived as bewildering sounds before Kanho was sent to clean the toilets. Kanho recalls lying sick at Tassajara and hearing the sangha chant the names of the ancestors across the valley, like the pulse of the world. Kanho offers a loose list of reasons: chanting teaches, honors ancestors, links Zen centers, builds sangha, serves devotion, and occupies the mind. Kanho ends with chanting the ancestors' names when cookies and computer games have failed, then closes with Oliver's "When Death Comes."

sentences.text: *Don't hesitate.
If you suddenly and unexpectedly feel joy, don't hesitate.
Give into it.
There are plenty of lives and whole towns destroyed or about to be.
We are not wise and not very often kind, and much can never be redeemed.
Still, life has some possibility left.
Perhaps this is its way of fighting back, that sometimes something happens better than all the riches or power in the world.
It could be anything, but very likely you notice it in the instant when love begins.
Anyway, that's often the case.
Anyway, whatever it is, don't be afraid of its plenty.
Joy is not made to be a crumb.*
I really love that poem.
Here we are at the closing session of our practice period.
It seems like yesterday in some ways and like so long ago in others.
In fact, I stood right over there and I declared proudly that I was going to go on a news fast during practice period.
And then the coronavirus happened.
So let me report that my news fast did not happen.
It was a very intentional decision.
In the beginning it was something that happened over there in China, and I was mostly interested in it because I have two friends who live in the general area where the outbreak happened.
So I was paying more attention to it than I usually would have.
But it's not like that anymore.
It's not something that is happening on the other side of the world.
Watching myself throughout this whole event, I came to the conclusion that as soon as I hear something, my brain says, "Good."
"Oh, that's terrible."
Good, bad, and it does this running commentary on everything.
It's quite interesting to watch.
This brain is a thought-producing, opinion-making machine.
News flash: the number of coronavirus infections worldwide is now exceeding 100,000.
Probably someone you know will die of it.
It's not on the other side of the world anymore.
Washington state is the hot spot in the U.S.
Don't touch your face.
Wash your hands.
Go shopping so you can deal with supply interruptions.
But don't be a hoarder.
Leave some toilet paper for some other people.
We are bombarded with news.
It also changes every day, and it changes depending on which channel you listen to.
So it's really good to get away from all that and come to sesshin.
I don't know about you, but I have this great feeling of relief to come in here, but not to shut out what happened, not to ignore it, but to be with everything in a different way.
Out there, there are so many words.
There are words in here too, but it's different.
So we turn to different words, to words we speak together, words we chant, words we repeat over and over again, sometimes knowing what we say, sometimes not.
I love the Heart Sutra, and I have no idea how often I have chanted that by now.
But I certainly remember the first time I chanted it.
How about you?
Do you still remember?
It was during my first visit to the Bellingham Zen practice group, now Red Cedar Zen Community, down in the old building.
I had read lots of books about Zen.
Those books were full of masters and students, koans, shouting, interesting interactions.
I definitely had expectations, and I definitely wanted koans.
So I came to the hall, I was shown how to sit, and then when that was over, someone put a chant book in my hand, and we chanted the Heart Sutra.
It was pretty incomprehensible stuff.
Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva is quite a mouthful.
Shariputra, Prajna Paramita, the Five Skandhas, and so on.
I was still trying to recover from "Gathe, Gathe, Para, Gathe, Parasam Gathe" when we launched into the Enmei Jukku Kannon Gyo.
Then I was sent off to clean the toilets.
And then I was told there was a meeting going on, and I was there for the first time, so could I please go away?
Yeah, those were the times.
Each year we have a theme that we carry through many talks in the year, and since we have done this for three or four years now, it's a time-honored tradition.
This year, in general, we will be talking about chanting and chants quite a bit, and Tim suggested that I give a little talk about why we chant.
This talk definitely does not cover all the reasons why we're chanting.
It doesn't cover your personal, private motivations, but it's actually quite interesting that we get together and chant the Heart Sutra.
People all over the world get together to chant the Heart Sutra and the other chants.
I'm assuming that we all have our favorites.
My personal favorites are Genjokoan and the Heart Sutra, definitely the Jewel Mirror Samadhi.
If we really get into it, we might even read a book or an internet article about a chant, and in between all that: "Oh, this is my favorite chant."
"I don't like that one so well."
"This does not make any sense."
The question remains, why do we chant at all?
We chant in English, in Sino-Japanese, in Pali.
We chant Dharanis whose meaning, if they ever had one, has been lost in the mists of time.
I think it is safe to make the statement that chanting is a ritual and a part of our spiritual practice.
My teacher, Norman Fischer, said this about spiritual practice.
You've been doing lots of good things for lots of good reasons for a long time now.
For your physical health, your psychological health, your emotional health, for your family life, and for your future success, for your economic life, for your community, for your world.
But spiritual practice is useless.
It doesn't address any of those concerns.
It's a practice that we do to touch our lives beyond all concerns, to reach beyond our lives to their source.
And I think that really applies to chanting too.
When I went to Tassajara for the first time, about six, seven years ago, I was living in the dorm right across from the zendo, and the first five days, I, like all the other newcomers, sat tangaryo.
That means you sit from morning to night.
You do get a break, a brief one after each meal, but other than that, you just sit.
No talks, no walking meditation.
Just sit.
And it's pretty tough, actually.
Oh, and you have oryoki meals, and you sit during those too.
So tangaryo was over, and I thought the hardest part was behind me.
But then I got really, really sick.
Even the eno, who usually said you can't sit through anything, relented.
I stayed in bed for a few days, waiting for my fever to break and to get better.
But something caught me by surprise.
I was so close to the zendo, I would hear the chanting.
It was really amazing, especially in the morning.
The sangha would chant the names of the ancestors, and the rhythm of the names just echoed through that valley.
To me, it was the pulse of the world.
It was very strange and beautiful, and I was deeply moved by it.
It spoke to me not as information, but as time.
The names became not the names of individuals, but, as warm hand to warm hand, the ancestors, one after the other, as time made visible, or in this case, audible.
I confess that since then, I had not spent much thought about the activity of chanting itself.
It is simply something we do here in the zendo, together, as a sangha, or at home, in my private practice.
So I'm quite grateful that I actually have a reason to take a look at the why.
So yes, why do we chant?
Here are some thoughts that came up for me.
And like I said before, this is definitely not a fixed list.
Chanting is teaching.

There are great, deep, essential teachings: the Heart Sutra, Merging of Difference and Unity, as Tim has been teaching us during the last week, Fukanzazengi, How to Sit, Genjokoan, which is my personal favorite.
Truly understanding and embodying even one of these texts, or even just a few lines, could really make a difference.
And it has made a difference in my life.
Sometimes, after years of chanting the same text over and over again, a phrase can open up, it can clarify a prior understanding, or open a new view.
Chanting can orient us towards practice.
I find that while I may understand the individual words, the meaning of texts, the living of it, may escape me for a very long time, before I see even a bit of a shape.
Do I need to mention Dogen at this point?
Another reason why we may chant is to appreciate our ancestors.
We chant in English, in Japanese, in Sino-Japanese, in Pali, and the Dharanis.
Nobody really knows if they are a language at all.
Maybe the Dharanis have always been purely sound meditation, or magical incantation, curing ills through sound alone.
When we chant the Heart Sutra in Japanese, we can chant it to pay respect to our Japanese ancestors.
The refuges in Pali bring us back all the way to the time and the land of the Buddha.
So by chanting in these languages, we are able to appreciate the long journey through space and time that the texts have experienced.
Another reason to chant is connection with other Zen centers.
The beauty of the Enmei Jukku Kannon Gyo, or the Shosaimyo Kichijo Dharani: they are the same no matter where we go.
They might be chanted at different speeds, but we will recognize these chants and we will be able to connect.
Then chanting can also be an expression of community.
We are rather solitary in our zazen, but when we chant together and when we move together in ritual, during service, during oryoki, we are sangha.
Maybe it is a little bit like kayaking, which we used to call a solitary team sport.

Yes, you are in your boat and you have to paddle it if you want to get somewhere, but when you are in trouble, there is someone who will fish you out of the cold water, someone you can lean on, someone who might help you get where you want to be.
Or still in kayaking, sometimes you hang together as the whole group in the evening and you quietly talk about your day, or you get pretty rowdy and have fun.
So we do have everything we need as sangha, but chanting helps us to synchronize and to walk the path of awakening with the support of our friends.
Last but not least, chanting can be a devotional practice.
The definition of devotional is religious, sacred, or spiritual.
Chanting as a devotional practice is fully entering into the chant, expressing the spiritual intention one holds.
Intellectual understanding is not at the core of this practice.
Rather, it is an opening to the potential, seen as ritual, seen as an activity, abandoning oneself to the practice without a second thought and without holding back.
I really feel this energy when we chant together, and it's truly lovely to be kokyo at sesshin too.
I also love that at the end of service, we do give this energy, this merit we have created, back to the world.
Every time we are able to practice generosity and compassion, we may think that the recipient of our generosity benefits.
In truth, the act of giving may benefit the giver the most.
Conventional thinking might say we don't give away much by dedicating our merit.
Nobody's ever gone shopping and paid with merit.
And yet, and yet, compassionately thinking of those who are ill, those who have died, those who have a need, helps us to develop these qualities.
Then there is chanting as meditation.
Chanting occupies the mind.
Thoughts do not stray too far from the activity at hand.
Needing to track the chant, either in print or, if you know it by heart, does require constant vigilance.
It is very hard to track and chant and have the mind occupied with other things.
Just like in meditation, where we stay in form, we chant together.
When the eno announces the Heart Sutra, we don't break out into some lullaby.
Or maybe I should say the probability for that is very, very low.
I do remember Norman once leading us into a chant and getting "Happy Birthday" back instead.
I always liked the expression on his face when something like that happens.
I do not know how to label my last category.

When I am down and out and have sat for as long as I can and I find that my heart remains on edge, I've eaten all the cookies I could find in the house, and maybe I've played computer games till my eyes bucked out, maybe I've tried every self-soothing trick I've ever learned, I've done it all and my heart is still on edge.
Sooner or later I have to stop all these distractions because they just lead to a deeper pit.
When I'm still staring into that abyss, the abyss of loneliness, depression, aggression, lack of connection, I go chant, maybe the names of the ancestors or the Heart Sutra.
I go lose myself for a while so I can find myself again.
Chanting the names of the ancestors, a human chain spanning 2,500 years, untold suffering and untold happiness, warm hand reaching out, holding warm hand.
I would also like to close with a poem, another Mary Oliver poem.
It is called "When Death Comes."
*When death comes like the hungry bear in autumn.
When death comes and takes all the bright coins from his purse to buy me and snaps the purse shut.
When death comes like the measle pox.
When death comes like an iceberg between the shoulder blades.
I want to step through the door full of curiosity, wondering what is it going to be like, that cottage of darkness.
And therefore I look upon everything as a brotherhood and a sisterhood and I look upon time as no more than an idea.

And I consider eternity as another possibility and I think of each life as a flower, as common as a field daisy and as singular and each name a comfortable music in the mouth, tending as all music does towards silence and each body a lion of courage and something precious to the earth.*
*When it's over I want to say all my life I was a bride married to amazement.
I was the bridegroom taking the world into my arms.
And when it's over I don't want to wonder if I have made of my life something particular and real.
I don't want to find myself sighing and frightened or full of argument.
I don't want to end up simply having visited this world.*
